analysis.title: US Daily: October FOMC Recap: Sticking to an Every-Other-Meeting Pace
key_insights: The FOMC left the funds rate unchanged at its October 28, 2026 meeting, a widely expected decision. Recent comments from Fed officials had pointed to a compromise of hiking every other meeting.
GS expects a second and final hike in December, which would leave the funds rate at 4-4.25%. A third hike in March is possible if inflation comes in higher than GS expects.

The main statement change was the addition of 'the accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine' the appropriate policy stance. GS reads it as a soft nod toward a slower pace of tightening, since it could imply decisions need more information than is available between consecutive meetings.

GS read Chairman Warsh's comments as balanced and consistent with both an every-other-meeting pace and a limited total number of hikes. His conclusion that 'policy is working' suggests to GS that he is likely to see a limited number of hikes as sufficient.

Warsh cited strong business investment growth, a pickup in job growth relative to last year, and jobless claims at 'the lowest level in generations'. He said neither he nor most other FOMC participants thought the economy was running too hot.

Asked why the Fed did not hike, Warsh said inflation compensation and inflation expectations had moved in the right direction and that the FOMC had already 'removed a dose of accommodation' at the last meeting.

Warsh said raising rates is already having an effect and that financial conditions have tightened but are not tight. GS says this matches how its own financial conditions index has evolved over the last two months.
Warsh gave the Fed's task forces a deadline of the end of 2026 and expects most to report by then. The FOMC would consider their conclusions and possible changes to Fed policy in 2027Q1.

The FOMC will keep eight meetings per year. Starting next fall, one meeting in 2027 and two meetings in 2028 will be devoted to broad monetary policy strategy, with no policy statement and no vote on the funds rate.
